Exercise A

Just Me and My Backpack

Read the text and choose the word that fits each gap. The bold verbs are passive forms — you will work with them in Exercise B.

Before you read — optional, not marked
This is just to get you thinking — you can leave it empty and it does not count towards your score.
Reading text

The view from the terrace of the Sydney Harbour Youth Hostel was amazing. Just across the water, the Opera House shone white in the sun. Jim from Britain, Tanya from New Zealand and Moshe from Israel had known each other for less than a day and were already great 1.

“Where do you want to go next?” Tanya asked. “I want to see the real outback,” said Jim. “I don’t want to walk around in a tour 2 like a typical tourist. Just me and my backpack.”

A tall young man with an Australian 3 was watering the plants nearby. His name was Mike and he was one of the owners of the hostel. “Sorry, I couldn’t help overhearing,” he said. “Tourists have been killed out there by the heat and by bushfires. Last week I spoke to a bloke who had been bitten by a snake on an outback tour. He was only saved because he was in a group and the guide called an air 4 with a satellite phone. Don’t go into the outback on your own, mate.”

“I love the beach,” said Tanya, “but I’m a bit 5 of box jellyfish.” — “Not here,” said Mike. “The water in Sydney is too cold for marine stingers. Up in Queensland, choose a beach where a net has been put up. If you stay inside the area that has been netted 6, you’ll be fine.”

“And sharks?” asked Moshe. Mike laughed. “Only three or four people a year are attacked by sharks. It’s much more 7 that you’ll be caught by a rip current. Hundreds of swimmers are swept out to sea by rips every year and some of them are never 8 again.”

“Thanks,” said Tanya. “That’s very comforting.”

Exercise B

Missing in Western Australia

All eight gaps need a passive form: am/is/are, was/were or has/have been + past participle. The time words in each sentence tell you which tense to choose.

Complete the news report

Bushwalker missing in Western Australia

1. A 19-year-old student from London since Thursday morning.

2. His mobile phone near an outback trail on Friday morning.

3. His parents and are flying to Perth tonight.

4. The search every evening at sunset and starts again at first light.

5. Every year thousands of foreign tourists by bushwalking, but not all of them understand the risks.

6. Last month an 18-year-old from Ireland alive after nine days in the outback.

7. “Never leave the trails unless you proper survival training before your trip,” a spokesperson said.

8. So far, no trace of the student .

Exercise C

Our Jim? — Active into Passive

Tanya and Moshe are chatting about the missing bushwalker. Keep the tense of the active sentence and choose the matching passive form. Items 7 and 8 come back from earlier units — the past perfect (Outback) and verb + infinitive (Ireland).

Rewrite in the passive

1. Nobody has seen him since Thursday.
He since Thursday.

2. The guy at the hostel had warned Jim not to go off alone.
Jim not to go off alone.

3. Somebody else told him that it was safe.
He that it was safe.

4. They’ll rescue this guy.
This guy .

5. They aren’t going to call off the search.
The search .

6. A snake didn’t bite him.
He by a snake.

7. We couldn’t photograph the sunset, because we the camera back at the hostel.

8. Mike advised Jim into the outback alone.

Exercise D

The Passive Infinitive

After a modal verb (can, must, should) and after want, hope, expect, would like and would prefer, the passive is (to) be + past participle: Some guests would like to be shown around the city.

What the guests at the hostel want

1. “Can you give us a room with a harbour view, please?”
Some guests would like a room with a harbour view.

2. “You’ll show us around the city, won’t you?”
They expect around the city.

3. “You’re going to take us to a barbie on the beach, right?”
They hope to a barbecue on the beach.

4. “Do you serve breakfast on the terrace?”
They want breakfast on the terrace.

5. “Can you wake us up for our flight tomorrow morning?”
They want up for their flight.

6. “I hope you’ll tell me about any parties around here.”
He hopes about any parties around here.

7. Some of the most dangerous animals in the world in Australia.

8. Not all the stories about the outback .

Exercise E

Writing: Safety Advice for Backpackers

You are working at the Sydney Harbour Youth Hostel for the summer. Write the safety page for the hostel website (6–8 sentences) that backpackers like Jim read before they book an outback trip or go swimming. Use at least four passive forms, and at least one passive infinitive.

Ideas you can use

• What can be found in the outback, and what should never be done alone.

• What has to be taken on a walk: water, a map, a satellite phone.

• Which beaches have been netted off, and where swimmers are swept out by rips.

• What guests can expect to be given or to be told at the reception desk.

You can use these: Every year ... are attracted by ... ... has been put up ... should never be done alone ... must be taken You can expect to be told ... Nobody wants to be bitten by ...
Your safety page
Aim for 6–8 sentences with at least four passive forms and one passive infinitive.
